Hi, I'd like to ask about switching rooms. My roommate and I have really different schedules.

You can add swipes online, you know. It's cheaper per meal than paying at the door.

Log into the student portal and look under dining services. It only takes a minute.

Let me check. What's your name?
Daniel Okafor.

Listen to an announcement in a classroom.

Before we start, a quick change to the midterm. Instead of the in-class exam we planned for next Wednesday, you'll write a take-home essay. I'll post the questions online on Monday morning, and you'll have until Friday at noon to submit. The essay should be about four pages. Listen to an announcement in the campus library.

Listen to a talk in a biology class.

Let's talk about hummingbirds and a problem they face every single night. A hummingbird's heart can beat more than a thousand times a minute while it's flying, and it burns energy faster than almost any other animal its size. During the day, that's fine, because it can feed on nectar every few minutes. But at night it can't feed at all. So how does it make it to morning without running out of fuel? The answer is something called torpor. Torpor is a bit like a very short hibernation. The bird's body temperature drops sharply, and its heartbeat slows to a fraction of its daytime rate. In this state, it uses only a tiny amount of energy. Now, torpor isn't free. A bird in torpor is almost completely unresponsive, so it can't escape from a predator. And waking up takes time, often twenty minutes or more, as the bird shivers its muscles to warm itself back up. That's why hummingbirds don't seem to enter torpor every night. They use it mainly when their energy reserves are low, for example, after a cold, rainy day when flowers were hard to find. In other words, it's an emergency tool, not a nightly habit.
Listen to a talk in a business class.

Today I want to look at a pricing strategy you've almost certainly experienced without noticing: the loss leader. A loss leader is a product that a store sells at a very low price, sometimes below what the store paid for it. That sounds like a bad business decision, right? Why would anyone sell something at a loss? The logic is that the cheap item gets customers through the door. Think of a supermarket that advertises milk or eggs at an unusually low price. People come in for the bargain, but once they're inside, very few walk out with only milk. They pick up bread, snacks, and cleaning supplies, and those items carry normal or even high profit margins. So the store loses a little on the milk and makes it back on everything else. Notice that stores usually choose everyday items for this, things people buy often and know the price of. If the price of milk drops, shoppers notice right away. A discount on something unusual, like a specialty spice, wouldn't attract nearly as many people. Of course, the strategy has risks. Some shoppers, sometimes called cherry pickers, buy only the discounted item and leave. If too many customers do that, the store really does just lose money.

Listen to a talk in a history class.

Today we're going to talk about early lighthouses. For thousands of years, sailors needed a way to find safe harbors at night. The first lighthouses were very simple. People lit large wood fires on hills or on top of stone towers near the coast. Sailors could see the fire from far away and know where land was. But fires had problems. They used a lot of wood, and they were hard to keep burning in wind and rain. Later, people used oil lamps and candles inside glass rooms at the top of the towers. These were easier to protect from the weather. Then, in the eighteen twenties, a French scientist designed a special glass lens. It made the light much brighter, so ships could see it from more than twenty miles away. This lens changed lighthouses all over the world.

Not a word. I've sent him three messages since Monday.

Listen to a conversation between a student and a study abroad advisor.

Listen to an announcement in a biology lab.

One more thing before you go. Several groups have been leaving the microscopes on the benches with the lights still running. Those bulbs aren't cheap, and the department won't keep replacing them forever. From now on, each group will sign out a microscope and sign it back in at the end of the session. Listen to an announcement on the campus radio station.

The psychology department is recruiting volunteers for a study on sleep and memory. Participants will wear a light wrist monitor for two weeks and complete a short online puzzle each morning. There's no lab visit beyond the first briefing. Those who finish the full two weeks receive a forty dollar bookstore voucher; partial completion, unfortunately, doesn't qualify. Spaces are limited, and the last round filled within days, so if you're interested, don't sit on it. The sign-up link is on the department's homepage.
Listen to a talk in an earth science class.

I'd like to clear up a misconception that trips up a lot of students: the idea that water always freezes at zero degrees Celsius. Pure water can actually stay liquid well below that point, down to around minus forty in some cases. We call this supercooled water. So what's going on? For ice to form, water molecules need to line up into a crystal, and that process has to start somewhere. In everyday life it almost always starts on something else, like a speck of dust, a scratch in a container, or a grain of pollen. These starting points are called nuclei. Without them, the molecules jostle around but never quite lock into place. This matters enormously for weather. Clouds high in the atmosphere are often full of supercooled droplets, simply because there aren't enough suitable particles for ice to form on. When a few ice crystals do appear, they grow at the expense of the surrounding droplets and can eventually become heavy enough to fall. In fact, much of the rain that reaches the ground begins its life as snow up there. And here's where it gets practical. Supercooled droplets that strike an airplane's wing can freeze on contact, which is why icing is taken so seriously in aviation. The wing itself, in effect, becomes the nucleus.

Listen to a talk in an art history class.

Today we're looking at a painting technique called true fresco, used in many of the great wall paintings of Renaissance Italy. In true fresco, the artist paints onto wet plaster. As the plaster dries, a chemical reaction locks the pigment into the wall itself, so the color becomes part of the surface rather than sitting on top of it. That's why some frescoes have lasted for five hundred years. But this technique put enormous pressure on the painter. Plaster stays workable for only about a day, so artists spread fresh plaster over just the section they could finish before it dried. Art historians call each of these sections a giornata, which is Italian for a day's work. If you look closely at some famous ceilings, you can actually see faint lines where one day's patch meets the next, and by counting them, scholars can estimate how long a painting took. Mistakes were also hard to fix. An error couldn't simply be painted over. The painter had to chip away the plaster and redo that section. Some artists added final details on dry plaster for convenience, but those touches tend to flake off over the centuries.
Listen to a talk in a music class.

Have you ever wondered why, at the start of a concert, the whole orchestra tunes to a single note played by the oboe? There are a few reasons, and they're partly practical and partly historical. First, the practical side. The oboe has a bright, penetrating sound that cuts through the room, so every player can hear it clearly, even from the back of the stage. Its pitch is also quite stable. Many string instruments drift out of tune as the hall warms up, but the oboe is less affected, and it's hard for an oboist to adjust its pitch much anyway. So it makes sense for everyone else to match the oboe rather than the other way around. Now the historical side. In the seventeenth century, when orchestras were taking shape, the oboe was one of the few wind instruments commonly included, and it often played the main melody. It became the natural reference point, and the habit stuck. Interestingly, when an orchestra performs with a piano, the situation changes. A piano can't be retuned in the middle of a concert, so the oboist tunes to the piano first and then passes that note on to everyone else.
Listen to a talk in an urban studies class.

Walk across almost any college campus and you'll find narrow dirt trails cutting across the grass, often right next to a paved sidewalk. Urban planners have a name for these: desire paths. They form when enough people decide that the official route isn't the one they actually want to take, usually because it's longer or less direct. Over time, the grass wears away and a path appears. For a long time, planners treated desire paths as a nuisance. They put up fences or planted bushes to block them. But more recently, many designers have started to see them as free information. A desire path is basically a record of how people really move through a space, which is something no survey can capture quite as honestly. Some universities have taken this idea to its logical conclusion. When they build a new quad, they plant grass everywhere and wait a year before laying any sidewalks. Then they pave the paths that students have worn into the ground. The result is a layout that matches real behavior, and people tend to stay on those sidewalks. Of course, not every desire path should be paved. Some cut through areas that are dangerous or ecologically sensitive, and there, redirecting people still makes sense.
Listen to a talk in a geology class.

So where do caves come from? Most of the large cave systems in the world form in limestone, and the main tool that carves them is surprisingly gentle: rainwater. As rain falls through the air and soaks through soil, it picks up carbon dioxide, which turns it into a very weak acid. On its own, this water wouldn't harm most kinds of rock. But limestone is different. It dissolves slowly in weak acid. The water seeps into tiny cracks in the limestone and widens them, very gradually. We're talking about a process that can take hundreds of thousands of years. Eventually, the cracks become channels, and the channels become passages large enough to walk through. Now, once a cave has formed, the process can partly run in reverse. When water carrying dissolved limestone drips from a cave ceiling, it releases some of its carbon dioxide into the air. That makes it deposit a tiny bit of the mineral it was carrying. Drip by drip, those deposits build up into the icicle-shaped formations called stalactites. Where the drops hit the floor, matching columns called stalagmites grow upward. So the same water that hollows out a cave also decorates it.
Listen to a talk in an economics class.

Today's concept is the network effect. A product has a network effect when it becomes more valuable to each user as more people use it. The classic example is the telephone. If you owned the only telephone in the world, it would be useless. Who would you call? But every new phone owner made everyone else's phone a little more useful. You see the same pattern today with messaging apps and online marketplaces. A marketplace with lots of sellers attracts buyers, and lots of buyers attract more sellers. Network effects have some important consequences. One is that markets with strong network effects often end up dominated by one or two big players. Once a platform has most of the users, it's very hard for a newcomer to compete, even with a better product, because people don't want to leave the place where everyone else already is. Economists call this lock-in. Another consequence is that companies in these markets are often willing to lose money for years. They give the product away or sell it cheaply, hoping to grow big enough that the network effect takes over. It's a risky bet. If they never reach that size, the money is simply gone.
Listen to a talk in a botany class.

Carnivorous plants, like the Venus flytrap or the pitcher plant, tend to fascinate people because they turn the usual food chain upside down. But I want you to think about why a plant would evolve to eat insects in the first place. After all, these plants still have green leaves and still make their own sugar through photosynthesis. They don't need insects for energy. What they need is nutrients, especially nitrogen. Carnivorous plants almost always grow in places like bogs and wet sandy soils, where nitrogen is extremely scarce. In those conditions, an insect is basically a tiny package of fertilizer. Catching and digesting one gives the plant nitrogen that its roots simply can't find in the ground. This also explains why you don't see carnivorous plants taking over forests or fields. Building traps and producing digestive fluids costs the plant a lot of energy. In rich soil, ordinary plants can get the same nutrients cheaply through their roots, and they grow faster. So carnivory only pays off where the soil is poor. Here's a practical tip if you ever keep one at home: don't give it regular plant fertilizer. Its roots aren't adapted to rich soil, and too much can actually kill it.
Listen to a talk in a world history class.

When people hear the term Silk Road, they often picture a single highway with caravans traveling all the way from China to the Mediterranean. That image is misleading in a couple of ways. First, it wasn't one road. It was a shifting web of routes, over land and by sea, that changed as empires rose and fell and as some passes became too dangerous to use. Second, very few individual traders ever traveled the whole length. Goods moved in relays. A merchant might carry silk a few hundred miles to a market town, sell it to another merchant, and head home. The silk would change hands many times before it reached its final buyer, getting more expensive at every stage. Oh, and the name itself is fairly recent. It was coined by a German geographer in the nineteenth century. The people who actually used these routes didn't call them that. And silk was only one item among many. Spices, glass, paper, horses, and metals all moved along the same networks. Arguably, the most important things that traveled weren't goods at all, but ideas: religions, technologies, and even diseases spread along these routes. So when historians talk about the Silk Road today, they really mean a whole system of exchange.
Listen to a talk in an astronomy class.

Here's a question that might seem simple: why do we always see the same side of the Moon? The Moon does rotate, but it turns exactly once for every trip it makes around Earth. Because those two motions match, the same face always points toward us. Astronomers call this tidal locking. It didn't start out this way. Billions of years ago, the Moon spun faster. But Earth's gravity pulls slightly harder on the near side of the Moon than on the far side, stretching it into a very slightly oval shape. These bulges acted like a brake. As the Moon rotated, Earth's pull kept tugging the bulge back into line, gradually slowing the spin until the rotation matched the orbit. Once that happened, there was nothing left to slow down, and the Moon settled into the state we see now. This isn't unusual, by the way. Many moons in our solar system are tidally locked to their planets. And the effect works both ways. The Moon is slowly lengthening Earth's day, too, though only by a tiny fraction of a second every century. So in the very distant future, Earth's days will be noticeably longer than they are today.
Listen to a talk in a psychology class.

I want to talk about a bias that shows up constantly in negotiations, and that's anchoring. Anchoring describes our tendency to rely too heavily on the first number we hear when making a judgment. In a common type of experiment, people are asked to estimate something, say the price of a used car, right after seeing a random number. Those who saw a high number tend to give higher estimates, even when they know the number had nothing to do with the car. The first figure acts like an anchor. People adjust away from it, but not nearly enough. In negotiation, this has a clear implication. Whoever names the first price often shapes the whole conversation. If a seller opens high, the final deal tends to land higher than it otherwise would, because the buyer's counteroffers are pulled toward that opening figure. That's why some negotiation coaches advise making the first offer, as long as you've done your research. But there's a catch. If your opening number is wildly unrealistic, you can lose credibility, and the other side may simply walk away. So the advice isn't to be outrageous; it's to be ambitious but defensible. And if the other party anchors first, one tactic is to openly set their number aside and refocus the discussion on objective information, like market prices.
Listen to a talk in an architecture class.

Let's look at how Gothic cathedrals managed to have such tall walls and enormous windows. Earlier churches in Europe, in what we call the Romanesque style, had thick, heavy walls with fairly small windows. That wasn't just a matter of taste. A stone roof, especially a vaulted one, pushes outward on the walls, and thick walls were needed to resist that push. If you cut big openings for windows, you weakened the walls, and the building could collapse. Gothic builders solved this with a few innovations working together. One was the pointed arch, which directs more of the weight downward rather than outward. Another was the flying buttress. Picture a stone arm reaching from the upper wall out to a heavy pillar standing outside the building. The buttress catches the outward push and carries it down to the ground, away from the wall. With the walls no longer doing all the work, builders could open them up and fill them with stained glass. So when you stand inside a great cathedral and see walls that seem to be made of colored light, remember that the secret is mostly on the outside, in those stone arms you can't see from within.
